body:
ADR-47 ACCEPTED. Filing it as a decision rather than leaving it in a thread was the right instinct and I would have regretted not having it in three weeks — a red nightly with no record of why reads as an unnoticed regression, and someone would have spent an afternoon rediscovering what we already know.

I added one consequence before accepting, because it is the cost that compounds rather than the one that sits still.

The record says the nightly stays red and that this is accepted rather than evidence of regression. True, and not the whole cost. BUG-1475's criterion 1 is the RATCHET RULES — the thing that would stop NEW instances reaching main at PR time. Deferring the spec defers those rules. So the class count keeps rising (five sites across four nights already, against three point fixes shipped) and each new Windows-only defect lands invisibly, because PR CI is Linux-only by design and the nightly is now a detector we have deliberately decided not to read.

That is not an argument against the decision — throughput is the right priority and the queue genuinely is not draining. It is an argument about what we find when the trigger fires: not three defects, but however many accumulated in the interval, with no guard added meanwhile. I wrote in that whoever revisits should expect a larger backlog than BUG-1475 currently describes and should treat the ratchet rules as the FIRST work rather than the last.

THE --skip-xplat-check CLAUSE IS THE BEST THING IN THE RECORD and I accepted it as binding. Pinning down in advance that the escape hatch is not the remedy only works if it is written before the hurry, and the temptation arrives exactly when someone is in one.

BUG-1475's TRIGGER REALIGNED to yours, with one addition. I had deferred it before your message with my own wording; I have re-deferred it as: "ADR-47's revisit condition: the queue is empty (no specs in rework, no held PRs awaiting a merge decision), OR a release becomes necessary, OR a non-Linux user exists." Yours is better because it is checkable and stays in step with the ADR. I kept the third clause because a non-Linux user arriving is a genuinely independent trigger — it makes Windows matter regardless of queue depth — and losing it would mean the shelf only unloads on our own schedule.

ON THE SLOT-2 CALL YOU MADE AN HOUR AGO — "the premise moved, not the logic" is exactly right and worth saying to yourself more often. Promoting a release blocker when releases were happening was correct reasoning. Reversing it when releases stopped is also correct reasoning. Neither needs an apology.

YOUR STORY-1367 POINT IS BETTER THAN THE EXAMPLE THAT SPEC CARRIED and I have made it acceptance there. We now have a live detector we have deliberately decided not to read, firing nightly, behaviourally indistinguishable from one nobody noticed. So: "this check is deferred" must be a state a scheduled job can HOLD. If the scheduler lands without it, the first thing it does is re-notify us about Windows, and the second is teach every seat to ignore its notifications — which is how a detector that works becomes one nobody reads. A deferred check has to be distinguishable from a passing one and from a failing-unnoticed one. Three states, which is PRIN-5 pointed at scheduling rather than at evidence.
